briefing.text: Every sample in this dataset (MBC_* samples, whole-exome with matched normals) is a metastasis: 143 HR+/HER2-, 51 HR-/HER2-, 14 HER2+ and 8 not determined. The tables hold no early breast cancer group to compare against. Check this by tabulating SAMPLE_TYPE against IHC_HER2 in data_clinical_sample.txt. Under the benchmark convention, a missing comparator does not make the hypothesis Not verifiable. The hypothesis concerns this study's own cohort (metastatic HR+/HER2- breast cancer) and its genes, so the label must be True or False. Compute the metastatic HR+/HER2- mTOR-pathway rate and compare it with a published primary/early HR+/HER2- reference (TCGA luminal BRCA, METABRIC) and with established biology. Say which of these decided the label.
briefing.reason: Without this, a team is likely to answer Not verifiable because no eBC group exists. Under the grading convention that answer would be wrong.

briefing.text: Approximate per-gene mutation rates in early/primary HR+ (TCGA luminal) breast cancer, for use as the external reference: AKT1 about 3-5%, PTEN mutation about 3-5%, TSC1, TSC2 and MTOR about 1-2% each. PIK3CA is about 35-45% in both primary and metastatic disease. Compare the metastatic rate gene by gene and for the pathway as a whole. Count one sample per patient. With only 143 HR+/HER2- samples, judge the size and direction of the difference against the reference, and do not rely on significance alone. (Not web-verified; from Bertucci et al. Nature 2019 and Razavi et al. Cancer Cell 2018.)
briefing.reason: The comparison has to be made against an external reference, so teams need concrete reference numbers and a warning about low statistical power.

briefing.text: Which genes count as the mTOR pathway decides the result, so fix the gene set before looking at any results. One example is PI3K/AKT/mTOR: PIK3CA, PIK3R1, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, PTEN, TSC1, TSC2, MTOR, RICTOR, RPTOR, STK11, INPP4B. Report per-gene rates and the any-gene pathway rate, each with and without PIK3CA. PIK3CA differs little between primary and metastatic disease, so it can hide differences in the other pathway genes.
briefing.reason: The choice of gene set and the PIK3CA question can change the direction of the comparison.

briefing.text: data_mutations.txt includes Silent, intronic and UTR variants. Restrict to nonsynonymous coding classes: Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift, Splice_Site and In_Frame indels. Exome sequencing also picks up passenger missense variants in large genes (MTOR, NF1, RICTOR), which inflates rates compared with curated, OncoKB-filtered references. As a sensitivity check, also report rates using only hotspot and truncating variants: PTEN and TSC1/2 truncations, and PIK3CA, AKT1 and MTOR hotspots.
briefing.reason: The filter must match the reference's filtering, or the comparison is biased.

briefing.text: Prevalence is the number of unique altered samples divided by all profiled HR+/HER2- samples (IHC_HER2 == 'HR+/HER2-', profiled by WXS according to data_gene_panel_matrix.txt). Keep samples with zero mutations in the denominator. Deduplicate by Tumor_Sample_Barcode for each gene and for the pathway, because PIK3CA double mutants and other multi-hit samples would otherwise be counted twice. Do not mix in HR-/HER2- or HER2+ samples, since their PI3K-pathway rates differ.
briefing.reason: Using the wrong denominator or counting the same sample twice distorts the prevalence estimate.

briefing.text: In breast cancer the mTOR pathway is often activated through copy-number changes, such as PTEN deep deletion or amplification of PIK3CA or AKT. Counting mutations alone may understate prevalence. data_cna.txt is available, so report rates both for mutations only and for mutations plus CNA, and say which one matches the reference being compared.
briefing.reason: The hypothesis says 'mutations', but published rates often include CNAs. Including or excluding CNAs can change the comparison.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume a recalled external TCGA luminal/HR+ primary rate is a valid eBC comparator for these exome calls, although platform, caller, depth, purity and variant-filtering differ; neither matched the variant classes or gene list of the reference to its own counting.

Both teams treat 'mTOR pathway' as a gene set they defined themselves (AKT1/PTEN/TSC1/TSC2/MTOR, +/- PIK3CA, +/- PIK3R1/RHEB/STK11/RICTOR); the label could depend on which set and whether PIK3CA, which is common in both settings, is counted.
Both teams treat the 143 HR+/HER2- metastases as one homogeneous cohort, pooling four trials (SAFIR01, SAFIR02, MOSCATO, SHIVA) and assuming one sample per patient is representative.
Both lean on a recollection of the source study's finding and on 'established biology', and neither has verified it.
unused_evidence: Freq_Variant_Allele_Normal and n_alt_count / n_ref_count in data_mutations.txt: these can flag germline or contaminated calls (e.g. germline PTEN/STK11/TSC variants). Neither team says it checked normal support for the mTOR-gene calls.
The dbSNP_RS / dbSNP_Val_Status columns can flag common polymorphisms among the counted missense variants. Neither team reports using them.

Team A did not use STUDY_ID: per-trial rates (SAFIR01/SAFIR02/MOSCATO/SHIVA) can show whether a single trial drives the excess. Team B stratified by trial but did not report whether the result held in each trial.
Low-level CNA values (-1/+1) are present alongside -2/+2. Both used only deep deletion or amplification. That is defensible, but whether shallow PTEN loss changes the direction was not reported.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A: under strict oncogenic curation the core rate falls to about 8.6%, which it calls 'near the primary level'. This is reported, not resolved, and it directly threatens the direction of the claim.

Team B: the eBC reference (~10%) is recalled and the binomial p of 0.048 is borderline. The result is not robust to a modest change in the reference rate, and Team B did not run a sensitivity analysis over plausible reference values.

Both teams: the comparison counts all nonsynonymous variants (or hand-curated ones) in metastases against a published primary rate that may count only drivers or a different gene list. That mismatch in counting rules was named but not fixed.
second_readings: 'Mutations in the mTOR pathway' may mean point mutations only, excluding CNAs, or it may mean pathway alterations including PTEN deletion and AKT amplification.

The pathway may or may not include PIK3CA (PI3K/AKT/mTOR versus mTOR-specific genes such as AKT1/PTEN/TSC1/TSC2/MTOR). PIK3CA prevalence is similar in eBC and mBC, so including it could dilute the difference.
'Higher prevalence' could mean any numerical excess or a statistically significant enrichment. With n=143 and no internal comparator, the two readings could lead to different labels.
challenge.verdict: I moderately trust the agreed answer. Both teams correctly saw that the hypothesis is about this study's cohort, and established biology fits enrichment in pretreated metastases. But the in-data support depends on a recalled, unverified primary reference and on loose variant counting: under strict filtering Team A's excess nearly disappears, and Team B's p-value is borderline. The answer should go out only if the direction holds once both sides are counted with the same rules.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your oncogenic-only rate (~8.6%) is 'near the primary level'. Recount the published primary reference using the same oncogenic-only rule and the same gene list as your curated metastatic count. Does the direction of the comparison still hold, and does that change your method or label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Compute the mTOR-pathway rate separately for each STUDY_ID (SAFIR01, SAFIR02, MOSCATO, SHIVA) within HR+/HER2-. Is the excess present in each trial, or is it driven by one trial, and does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: For every counted mTOR-pathway variant, check n_alt_count and Freq_Variant_Allele_Normal (normal support) and dbSNP status. Do any calls look germline or polymorphic, and does removing them change the rate or your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your binomial test against ~10% gives p=0.048. Re-run it over a range of plausible reference rates and with the reference's own variant classes and gene list applied to your counts. At what reference rate does the result stop exceeding it, and does that change how you weigh the data against the source-study recollection?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Apply a driver/oncogenic-only filter (the Hotspot column is uninformative, so curate by hand) to the mTOR-pathway calls in the 143 HR+/HER2- samples. Does the rate stay above the reference you used, and does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: For each counted mTOR-pathway variant, check n_alt_count / Freq_Variant_Allele_Normal and dbSNP_RS. Are any calls supported in the matched normal or known polymorphisms, and does excluding them change the rate?
QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You stratified by trial. Report the per-STUDY_ID HR+/HER2- rate. Does every trial exceed the reference, or does the excess depend on one trial?

In large published primary (early) HR+/HER2- breast cancer exome or panel cohorts, what are the reported per-gene mutation frequencies for AKT1, PTEN, TSC1, TSC2, MTOR and PIK3CA, and which variant classes (all nonsynonymous vs oncogenic only) does each frequency count?
questions.why: Both teams compared against reference rates they recalled but did not verify, and the label depends on that comparison. Knowing the actual rates and their counting rules would show whether the metastatic excess is real.

questions.question: Do published comparisons of metastatic versus primary HR+/HER2- breast cancer genomics report enrichment of mTOR-pathway (AKT1, PTEN, TSC1/2, MTOR) alterations in metastases, and is that enrichment seen for point mutations alone or mainly when copy-number loss is included?
questions.why: This tests the 'established biology' that both teams relied on and decides which reading of 'mutations' supports the claim.

findings.question: In large published primary (early) HR+/HER2- breast cancer exome or panel cohorts, what are the reported per-gene mutation frequencies for AKT1, PTEN, TSC1, TSC2, MTOR and PIK3CA, and which variant classes (all nonsynonymous vs oncogenic only) does each frequency count?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: all 3 research-gateway calls (search x2, contents x1) failed with HTTP 502 / Exa 403, so I read no page and verified nothing. Unverified recall, for orientation only: primary HR+/HER2- BC rates are PIK3CA ~35-45%, AKT1 ~3-7% (mostly E17K), PTEN mutation ~3-5%, MTOR ~1-3%, TSC1 ~1%, TSC2 ~1%. TCGA (Nature 2012) counts all nonsynonymous somatic mutations. MSK-IMPACT primary-vs-metastatic comparisons (Razavi, Cancer Cell 2018) count OncoKB oncogenic/likely oncogenic variants only. My recollection is that those comparisons found AKT1, PTEN and the other mTOR-pathway genes modestly enriched in metastases and PIK3CA about the same. Match the counting rule to the reference you compare against.
